title: Agent Configuration Layering Reference
summary: Locate and reconcile system, managed, user, workspace, local, and task-level AI tool configuration without guessing which layer wins.
prerequisites: The selected tool's current configuration documentation
Access to inspect the effective workspace configuration
Authority to change the intended configuration layer

sections.title: Map layers before resolving a conflict
paragraphs: AI tools use different names and precedence rules for managed policy, user settings, workspace configuration, local overrides, instruction files, rules, commands, and runtime flags. Do not assume a precedence order transfers between products. Use the current product documentation and inspect the effective configuration where the tool exposes it.

Before changing anything, record the tool, version, working directory, operating system, account or tenant scope, and the setting key. Classify each candidate source by owner, scope, sensitivity, sharing behavior, documented precedence, and enforcement point.

A working directory can change which project or workspace file is discovered. Environment variables and command-line arguments can also affect the result. The exact discovery and key-specific behavior is version-dependent unless the product documentation states otherwise. Treat an unverified discovery rule as UNKNOWN, not as a missing file.

code.label: Configuration precedence worksheet
code.code:
Task: [CONFIGURATION OUTCOME OR CONFLICT]
Scope: [TOOL, VERSION, WORKSPACE, USER, AND EXECUTION ENVIRONMENT]
Permissions: [LAYERS THIS OPERATOR MAY INSPECT OR CHANGE]
Layer inventory: [MANAGED | USER | WORKSPACE | LOCAL | INSTRUCTIONS | FLAGS]
Owner and sharing: [LAYER -> OWNER -> PRIVATE OR COMMITTED]
Documented precedence: [OFFICIAL RULE OR UNKNOWN]
Effective observation: [VALUE, SOURCE, AND REPRODUCER]
Stop conditions: [MANAGED POLICY, SECRET EXPOSURE, UNKNOWN PRECEDENCE, OR WIDER IMPACT]
Verification: [FRESH SESSION, EFFECTIVE CONFIG, MINIMAL TASK, AND DIFF]
Recovery: [RESTORE THE ONE CHANGED LAYER AND REPEAT THE REPRODUCER]

sections.title: Change the owning layer, not every copy
paragraphs: Reproduce the conflict with a minimal, non-sensitive task. Record the value at each applicable layer and the effective result. Change only the layer owned by the intended audience. Do not copy personal paths, account identifiers, or credentials into shared configuration merely to override a local problem.

A scalar setting usually has one effective value, but the winning source and precedence are product- and key-specific. A list setting may be replaced, appended to, merged, or subject to exceptions. Do not infer list behavior from scalar behavior. Confirm the key-specific rule in the current schema or documentation. If it is not documented, record the merge behavior as UNKNOWN and verify with a harmless test.

Managed policy is an administrative boundary. If local configuration cannot override it, document the conflict and escalate to its owner. Do not bypass it with an undocumented flag, copied configuration, or altered identity.

code.label: Completed fictional conflict record
code.code:
Task: Keep spinner tips disabled for one operator in one project.
Tool and scope: Claude Code, documented settings example, one project, one user.
Setting: spinnerTipsEnabled, scalar boolean.
Initial inputs:
  User ~/.claude/settings.json: {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false}
  Shared project .claude/settings.json: {"spinnerTipsEnabled":true}
  Private project .claude/settings.local.json: key absent
  Managed settings: not present in this fictional record
  Environment variables and CLI arguments: not used
Documented owner and precedence: The shared project value overrides the user value for this project. The private project file is the scoped owner for a personal project-only preference and overrides the shared project value, according to the cited Claude Code documentation.
Exact proposed one-layer change:
  Add {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false} to .claude/settings.local.json.
Expected observation: This operator sees spinner tips disabled in this project; the shared file remains true for collaborators. This is an expected result from documentation, not an observed client run.
Stop decision: Stop before changing if the file is shared, if managed settings are present, if the key is not supported by the installed version, or if the effective result cannot be attributed to one source.
Verification: Inspect /status for setting sources, start a fresh session, perform the minimal UI observation, and review the one-file diff.
Recovery: Remove only the added local key, reopen the client, and repeat the minimal observation.
No credentials, permissions, purchases, or authorization controls are changed.

sections.title: Tool lookup: documented places to inspect
paragraphs: Claude Code: The documented user file is ~/.claude/settings.json. Shared project settings are in .claude/settings.json, and private project settings are in .claude/settings.local.json. The private project file is intended for personal preferences and overrides shared project settings. Managed settings can restrict customization, with documented security-key exceptions. Use /status to show setting sources. Use /config to edit selected personal settings, not as a claim that every key is edited there. Lists often merge, but exceptions exist, and environment-variable precedence is key-specific. Confirm the installed version and platform-specific discovery behavior before applying a path literally.

Gemini CLI: The documented user file is ~/.gemini/settings.json and a workspace file is .gemini/settings.json. The settings dialog opens with /settings. The separate configuration reference documents low-to-high configuration as defaults, system defaults file, user file, project file, system settings file, environment variables, and command-line arguments. System settings file paths include C:/ProgramData/gemini-cli/settings.json on Windows and /etc/gemini-cli equivalents on Linux. This hierarchy describes configuration precedence, not absolute authorization. Key-specific restrictions and the current version still matter.

Continue is a client, not a model vendor. Its current local user configuration is ~/.continue/config.yaml, or %USERPROFILE%/.continue/config.yaml on Windows. The Local Config dropdown cog opens the file, and saved IDE configuration auto-refreshes. The cited documentation identifies config.json, .continuerc.json, and config.ts as legacy or deprecated. It does not establish a modern universal user-versus-workspace precedence rule. Do not force Continue into the Claude Code or Gemini CLI hierarchy. Inspect the active configuration UI and current schema instead.

code.label: Lookup commands and documented UI entry points
code.code:
Claude Code:
  /status
  /config

Gemini CLI:
  /settings

Continue:
  Open the Continue panel, choose the Local Config dropdown, and select the cog.

These entry points identify documented inspection or editing surfaces. They do not prove that a setting is authorized, supported by every version, or effective for every key.

sections.title: Separate instructions, settings, and authorization
paragraphs: Instruction files and prompts tell a client how to behave or what context to use. Settings configure client features, paths, models, or interaction preferences. Neither category automatically grants operating-system access, identity privileges, network access, repository write access, or server-side authorization.

A repository instruction can request that a tool avoid a command, but it cannot replace a file-system permission. A local setting can change a display preference, but it cannot legitimately override an organization-managed restriction. A command-line argument can affect one invocation without proving that a durable setting changed.

When examining a conflict, write down the enforcement point: client behavior, local process, operating system, identity provider, network, or server. If the claimed outcome depends on a control outside the client, verify that control separately. Never test this distinction by attempting a permission bypass.

sections.title: Worked scenario: trace a harmless preference
paragraphs: Scenario: an operator wants spinner tips disabled only in the current project. The shared project file enables them for everyone, while the operator's user file disables them globally. The desired scope is one operator and one project, so changing the shared file would be too broad and changing the user file would affect other projects.

The owning layer is the private project file, .claude/settings.local.json. It is private to the operator and scoped to the project. The exact proposed change is to add the scalar key {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false} there, leaving both existing files unchanged.

Reasoning: the user value is false, the shared project value is true, and the private project value is initially absent. The documented Claude Code example supports the private project value as the personal project-only override. The expected result is false for this operator in this project. No client was executed for this material, so this is documented expected behavior, not an observed outcome.

Verification should use /status to inspect setting sources, a fresh session, the smallest UI observation that distinguishes true from false, and a diff showing exactly one changed file. If the result is different, stop. Check version, working directory, managed settings, environment variables, and command-line arguments before changing another layer. Restore the one changed key if the scope is broader than intended.

sections.title: Learner exercise: changed input and answer
paragraphs: Change the scenario as follows: the operator now wants spinner tips enabled only for this project, while keeping them disabled in all other projects. The shared project file contains {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false}, the user file contains {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false}, and the private project file is empty.
Exercise: identify the owning layer, state the exact one-layer change, predict the effective value in this project, and name one observation that would make you stop rather than add another override.

Answer: the owning layer is .claude/settings.local.json. Add exactly {"spinnerTipsEnabled":true} to that file. This private project override is needed because the user and shared project values are both false. The expected effective value for this operator in this project is true, while the user and shared project files remain false elsewhere. Make no changes to the user or shared project files.

A response that says the effective value is already true is incorrect for this changed input. A response that edits the user file has the wrong scope. A response that edits the shared file changes collaborators' behavior. Stop if /status attributes the value to managed settings, if the active working directory is not the intended project, if the installed version does not document the key, or if an environment variable or command-line argument is supplying an unexplained value.

Causal rubric: full credit requires identifying the private project layer, the exact boolean value true, project-only scope, and a valid stop condition. Penalize edits to the user or shared layer. Also require recognition that the private override is necessary in this scenario. A response that claims the value grants permission confuses a UI setting with authorization.

sections.title: Learner exercise: recognize when no edit is needed
paragraphs: A second operator wants spinner tips disabled in this project. The user file contains {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false}, the shared project file contains {"spinnerTipsEnabled":false}, and the private project file is empty. The documented effective value is therefore false for this project.

Answer: make no configuration change. Credit the response if it identifies the effective value as false, records that both applicable defined sources agree, and preserves the empty private project file. The smallest needed change is no edit. An unnecessary private override is not required and should not receive full credit.

Before awarding credit, the learner should state how the result would be checked, such as using /status and a fresh session where supported. If the observed source or value differs from the documented expectation, stop and investigate the tool version, working directory, managed settings, environment variables, and command-line arguments.

sections.title: Expected evidence and verification
paragraphs: Expected evidence includes the tool and version, official configuration reference, applicable layers and owners, documented precedence or an explicit UNKNOWN, a secret-safe reproducer, the one changed layer when a change is necessary, and the effective result in a fresh session. Verify that shared configuration contains no user-specific path, account, tenant, or credential.

Distinguish documented expectations from observations. No real Claude Code, Gemini CLI, or Continue client was executed for this material. The worked scenario, learner exercises, and offline fixture therefore do not prove deployed product behavior. Record an observation only after running the named client and version in the named workspace.

If behavior changes outside the target workspace or the effective value cannot be explained, stop and restore the changed layer from the recorded baseline. Restart the relevant client, reopen the workspace, and rerun the minimal reproducer before proceeding. If the setting is a list, record whether the observed result is replacement, concatenation, deduplication, or another key-specific rule. If that rule cannot be established, record UNKNOWN.

sections.title: Offline teaching exercise: trace a declared layering model
paragraphs: The following Node.js 22 exercise is dependency-free and intentionally small. It reads a fixture containing ordered layers and resolves a scalar key by taking the last defined value. That rule is a teaching contract for this fixture only. It is not an emulation, compatibility test, or validation of Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Continue, or any deployed product.

The exercise also reports every candidate source, making ownership and scope visible. It has a negative case for a missing key. It does not edit files, invoke a client, change global settings, inspect secrets, or test authorization.

code.label: Save as trace-layering.mjs

sections.title: Offline exercise inputs
paragraphs: Create initial.json with the following exact contents, then create changed.json by changing only the privateProject value from false to true. The fixture order is deliberately stated in the file. It is not a claim about any client product's order.

sections.title: Offline exercise commands
paragraphs: Save the JavaScript code as trace-layering.mjs. Run the initial and changed fixtures, then request a key that no layer defines. The negative case must exit with status 1 and must not print a WINNER or EFFECTIVE line.

code.code:
node trace-layering.mjs initial.json
node trace-layering.mjs changed.json
node trace-layering.mjs initial.json missingKey

paragraphs: For the missingKey command, the process exits with status 1. Standard output contains the source report, and standard error contains the error. Neither stream contains a WINNER or EFFECTIVE line.

sections.title: Source boundaries and unresolved questions
paragraphs: The Claude Code settings documentation supports the documented file locations, private project override behavior, managed settings boundary, /status, /config, list-setting exceptions, and key-specific environment-variable precedence. It does not establish one universal merge rule for all keys or one universal discovery rule across operating systems, worktrees, and versions.

The Gemini CLI settings documentation supports the user and workspace locations and /settings. The Gemini configuration reference supports the documented low-to-high source order and example system paths. It does not establish that every setting accepts every source, flag, or scope, and configuration precedence is not the same as absolute authorization.

The Continue configuration documentation supports the current local config path, Local Config cog, auto-refresh behavior, and legacy labels. It does not prove a modern universal workspace-versus-user precedence hierarchy. Continue must therefore be investigated through its active UI and current schema rather than assigned another tool's order.

UNKNOWN: key-specific scalar and list merge rules for all three tools; complete instruction-file versus settings precedence; exact version, environment, and working-directory discovery effects; and whether the offline fixture's output corresponds to any deployed client. Establish these with the installed client's dated documentation, effective-configuration inspection, and a harmless minimal reproducer. No such clients were executed for this material.
